title: Hemorrhagic shock and the canine spleen
why_this_matters: A dog's contractile spleen changes how blood loss shows up, so a human clinician's read of early vital signs and blood counts can understate how much blood a dog has lost.

what_changes_from_human.point: The dog has a large, contractile spleen that can modify its response to bleeding, unlike the human spleen.
A blood count that has not yet fallen does not rule out major blood loss in a dog.
Stopping the bleeding comes first. Fluids are supportive, and blood products are preferred for severe hemorrhage where available.

takeaway: A dog's spleen can hide early blood loss, so control the bleeding and do not be reassured by a normal early blood count.

compare.human: The human spleen does not act as a large blood reservoir under hemorrhage.
compare.canine: The dog has a large, contractile spleen that can modify its cardiovascular response to bleeding. A letter citing other studies describes spleens of the pig, cat and dog (unlike the human) sequestering a large share of blood volume (up to 20 to 25%) and autotransfusing a substantial volume under severe hemorrhage. The figures come from a letter, not a primary study.
compare.implication: Expect a compensated-looking dog early in major blood loss, then a fast decline once splenic reserve is used.

compare.human: Hemoglobin and hematocrit typically lag behind acute blood loss until fluid shifts or resuscitation dilute the blood.
compare.canine: In conscious dogs with intact spleens bled 41% of blood volume, hemoglobin did not change; the authors attributed this to splenic contraction adding concentrated red cells, later diluted by extracellular fluid moving into the vessels.
compare.implication: A normal early hemoglobin or hematocrit does not exclude major blood loss in a dog.

compare.canine: All 10 splenectomized conscious dogs died after 41% blood volume hemorrhage in one experimental study, and splenectomized dogs showed greater loss of left ventricular performance in another.
compare.implication: The spleen contributes to survival of severe hemorrhage in dogs. Splenic injury or splenectomy changes what to expect.

compare.human: Tachycardia, low blood pressure, raised lactate and base deficit.
compare.canine: The physiologic response to whole blood loss in dogs is characterized clinically by increased heart rate, decreased systolic blood pressure and increased shock index, and biochemically by increased lactate and lower base excess.
compare.implication: The same markers apply; read them together with the spleen effect above.

compare.human: Hemorrhage control first, with blood products favoured over large-volume crystalloid in severe hemorrhage.
compare.canine: A review supports prioritizing hemorrhage control with judicious crystalloid, then early consideration of platelets, plasma and red cells. Another proposes hemostatic resuscitation for dogs, using plasma and whole blood while minimizing crystalloids and colloids, and states more work is needed.
compare.implication: Do not treat fluid volume as a substitute for hemorrhage control. Availability of canine blood products is the practical limit; see the blood-groups module.
